solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Bulb switched off, heading for darkness in Irish house

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so these letters go within the outer word

parts.note: the Dail is the lower house of the Irish parliament

indicators.note: something switched has been changed around, so the letters swap places

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its front, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of darkness

explanation.surface: A light bulb has been turned off, leaving darkness in an Irish home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bulb' reads as a light bulb, but it is the plant kind. The Dail (Dail Eireann) is Ireland's lower house of parliament, a common crossword source for DAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: The daffodil grows from a bulb, so the flowering plant is an example of the gardener's sense of that word.

clue.text: Set aside loads, saving fifty

indicators.note: to save something is to keep it safe within, so one piece holds another

parts.note: 'a lot' means loads
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone puts away plenty of money while managing to save fifty pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: L goes inside A LOT, just after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot is to assign or earmark a share for a particular purpose, which is setting it apart.

clue.text: I worked for spinster

indicators.note: worked material has been kneaded and reshaped, so the letters are formed anew

parts.note: the letters as printed, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone recalls having once been employed by an unmarried woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the single letter-word 'I', which hides in plain sight as the subject of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar the pronoun used by a speaker about themselves belongs to the singular first-person category.

clue.text: Drunk reacted, grabbing new bottle

indicators.note: to grab something is to take hold of it, so one piece clutches another inside
a drunk person staggers about out of order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A drunk responded by snatching a fresh bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: N joins the letters of REACTED and the whole lot is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A decanter is a glass vessel with a stopper, used for serving wine or spirits, so it is a kind of bottle.

clue.text: Load washing line and don't hold back

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: peg every piece of laundry up to dry
second meaning: the idiom for being completely uninhibited

explanation.surface: Instructions for doing the laundry: fill the line and keep nothing back.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is the idiom taken literally, as advice about pegging out a wash.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase means behaving with total freedom and candour, without restraint or reserve.

clue.text: Glossy dish for bird

parts.note: a glossy is a magazine printed on shiny paper, shortened to mag
a pie is a baked dish

explanation.surface: A shiny plate of food intended for a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glossy' looks like an adjective but is a noun: a glossy magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: The magpie is a black-and-white member of the crow family, common across Britain.

clue.text: Figure inspired by scooter rider was daydreaming

indicators.note: something inspired is breathed in, so one piece is drawn inside another

parts.note: Mods were a 1960s British youth subculture known for riding motor scooters
one is a number, a figure

explanation.surface: A person whose imagination was sparked by a scooter rider sat daydreaming.
explanation.walkthrough: A Mod was a member of a 1960s British youth cult whose emblem was the Vespa or Lambretta scooter.
explanation.definitionFit: To moon about is to wander listlessly lost in thought, so mooned matches past-tense idle dreaming.

clue.text: Come together when member stands up

indicators.note: in a down entry, standing up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a leg is a limb, or member, of the body

explanation.surface: A group finally unites once one of its members rises to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a club member, but it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: When a team or idea gels it sets firmly into a cohesive whole, as a jelly sets.

clue.text: Puck on stage making a hit

parts.note: Puck is the mischievous sprite of A Midsummer Night's Dream, an imp
the stage as a profession means acting

explanation.surface: An actor playing Puck in the theatre turns out to be a hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puck' could be the ice hockey disc, which suits 'hit'; here it is Shakespeare's sprite.
explanation.definitionFit: Impacting means striking or colliding with force, which is a literal way of landing a blow.

clue.text: Turning circle for religious minister

indicators.note: turning things over changes their arrangement, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A spinning ring is meant for a priest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning circle' reads as a car's turning circle, but the first word only tells you to rearrange the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleric is a member of the clergy, an ordained priest or pastor who serves a church.

clue.text: Writer has dropped bap into drink

indicators.note: something dropped falls down into whatever lies beneath it, ending up enclosed
into means going inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: to tope is an old verb meaning to drink heavily
a bap is a soft British bread roll

explanation.surface: An author has let a bread roll fall into a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: A bap is a soft round bread roll in Britain. Anthony Trollope was the Victorian novelist of the Barsetshire books.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Trollope was a prolific nineteenth-century English novelist, so he is an instance of an author.

clue.text: Leave that text penned by best etymologist

indicators.note: something penned is enclosed as in a pen, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: An etymologist's note asking that their wording be left alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penned' looks like 'written', which suits the scholar, but it means enclosed.
explanation.definitionFit: Stet is the proofreader's Latin instruction, 'let it stand', telling the printer to ignore a correction and keep the original.

clue.text: Toad observing rabbit on rabbit, say

parts.note: to rabbit on is British slang for chattering endlessly, as is to natter
a jackrabbit is a kind of hare, so a jack is an example of a rabbit-like animal

explanation.surface: A toad watches one rabbit perched on top of another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit on' is British slang for talking at length; the first rabbit is a verb, the second an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The natterjack is a European species of toad, notable for its yellow back stripe and loud call.

clue.text: Otherwise futile, jab is warranted

indicators.note: otherwise means in a different way, so the letters take a different order

parts.note: the letters as printed, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An injection that would otherwise be pointless is justified after all.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder runs across the comma: three words, eleven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something warranted has proper grounds or reasons behind it, which is exactly what can be defended as justifiable.

clue.text: I'm off food, effectively

parts.note: fare is food served, as in a menu's bill of fare
to do something effectively is to do it well

explanation.surface: Someone announces they have more or less gone off their food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm off food' sounds like losing an appetite; 'I'm off' is a parting remark on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying goodbye as you leave is a parting salutation, the same job as the announcement of departure.

clue.text: Strapping on end of sleeve for astronaut

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing placed on another sits above it, fixing the order

parts.note: the arm emerges from the end of a sleeve
strapping means big and powerful

explanation.surface: A spacesuit is being strapped at the cuff for an astronaut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strapping' looks like fastening a strap; it is the adjective for a sturdy build. It is placed after the limb, as 'on' directs in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil Armstrong commanded Apollo 11 and was the first person to walk on the Moon.

clue.text: Fielding error?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a close catching position beside the wicket-keeper in cricket

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it looks like a dropped catch; apart, one word is a cricket fielding position and the other a mistake. Slip is a fielder standing beside the wicket-keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a cricket position for fielders near the batter and a minor lapse or blunder.

clue.text: Disorder seen in Mediterranean island after uprising, come together

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising up means reading bottom to top, so the combined letters run backwards
what is seen in a place is inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: Elba is the island where Napoleon was first exiled
a mess is a state of disorder

explanation.surface: Chaos on a Mediterranean island after a revolt, as people gather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uprising' suggests a revolt on the island, but in a down entry it means the letters read upwards. The disorder goes in near the island's end, before the turn.
explanation.definitionFit: To assemble is to gather in one place, so people meeting up are joining together.

clue.text: Name of authors wrong, though not entirely

indicators.note: not entirely means incomplete, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a synonym of wrong

explanation.surface: An authors' names have been listed wrongly, at least in part.
explanation.walkthrough: Kingsley Amis and his son Martin Amis were both British novelists, so one surname covers two authors.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley and Martin, father and son, both wrote celebrated novels, so the surname belongs to a pair of writers.

clue.text: Seaside town contains property, but no hospital

parts.note: to contain is to have within

indicators.note: 'but no' says something is left out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: one's things are one's belongings or property
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A coastal resort has plenty of real estate but lacks a hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contains' looks like a container signal, but it simply supplies HAS. Hastings is a resort on England's south coast in East Sussex.
explanation.definitionFit: Hastings is a resort town on the English Channel coast, famous for the 1066 battle nearby.

clue.text: Gleeful as a grasshopper?

parts.note: surface reading: cheerful and lively
setter's reading: like an insect that makes a high trilling call

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: the adjective for being bright and cheerful also describes a creature that makes short shrill sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheerful and lively in spirit, the word comes from the bright trilling of birds and insects.

clue.text: Ancient ring may have gone with these rocks, unknown number visiting

indicators.note: a visitor comes inside, so one letter is placed among the others
to rock something is to shake it about, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
n is the algebra letter for an unknown number

explanation.surface: An ancient stone circle may have disappeared along with its rocks while an unknown number of people visited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocks' looks like the stones of the monument, but it is the verb that shakes the letters of 'gone' and 'these' once N has joined them.
explanation.definitionFit: Stonehenge is the prehistoric circle of standing stones on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire.

clue.text: Measure certain charity boxes

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so the letters sit inside the phrase

parts.note: letters across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Assessing particular collection tins used by a charity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxes' looks like collection boxes, a noun, but it is the verb meaning encloses.
explanation.definitionFit: An inch is a unit of length in the imperial system, one twelfth of a foot.

clue.text: Scale that's cold on fin, perhaps

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing on another sits above it, fixing the order

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
a fish's fin works as a limb; 'perhaps' marks it as an example

explanation.surface: A fish scale feels chilly on its fin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scale' and 'fin' set up a fish, but scale is the verb meaning to ascend.
explanation.definitionFit: To scale a wall or mountain is to ascend it, going up by hands and feet.

clue.text: A good time cut short by reluctant Prince Charming

indicators.note: cutting something short trims its end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: loth is a variant spelling of loath, unwilling
taken as written
a riot is a hugely enjoyable time, as in 'we had a riot'

explanation.surface: A fairy-tale hero's fun is curtailed because he is unwilling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' places the reluctant piece before the rest. Loth is an accepted British spelling of loath.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lothario is a seducer of women, named after a rake in an eighteenth-century play, so a smooth ladies' man.

clue.text: Chicken afterwards, no starter

indicators.note: a starter is what comes first, so the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: then means afterwards

explanation.surface: A meal of chicken as the main course, having skipped the first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' looks like a first course alongside 'chicken', but it means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A hen is a female domestic fowl, the bird most people mean by chicken.

clue.text: Spool bouncin' up and down

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a reel for thread
second meaning: moving up and down, with the final g clipped as the apostrophe in the clue shows

explanation.surface: A cotton reel jumping about.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped g in 'bouncin'' tells you the second meaning drops its g too.
explanation.definitionFit: A bobbin is a cylinder that holds thread for sewing or weaving, and bobbin' is casual speech for rising and falling.

clue.text: Department in New York bringing in head of corporation on time

indicators.note: in an across entry, being on another piece means being joined to it, here placed after

parts.note: an age is a period of time

indicators.note: bringing something in takes it inside, so the outer letters wrap around it

parts.note: NY is the standard abbreviation for New York

indicators.note: the head of something is its top, so only its first letter is used

parts.note: first letter of corporation

explanation.surface: A government department in New York hires a company's boss, punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: The time piece comes first, with the New York letters, holding the C, joined on after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A government agency is an administrative body or branch, such as the CIA, so a department of state.

clue.text: By three, thoroughbred finally prepared — for this race?

indicators.note: something prepared has been made ready and reworked, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of thoroughbred
taken as written, placed at the end

explanation.surface: A racehorse is readied by three o'clock for a big race.
explanation.walkthrough: BY is written first in the clue but goes last in the answer. The Derby is the famous flat race for three-year-olds run at Epsom in England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Derby at Epsom Downs is Britain's most prestigious flat horse race, run each June by three-year-old thoroughbreds.
